newsitem.title: INDIA: India says undecided on foreign equity in media.
newsitem.headline: India says undecided on foreign equity in media.

text.p: The Indian government, under fire from communist partners over a proposal to allow foreign equity into the broadcasting sector, said on Friday that the plan was still under consideration.
"Our government has an open mind. It is for the people to decide, the MPs will have to decide," Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy told reporters.
"The left parties have some objections. I would like to assure them that their objections will fully be taken note of," Reddy said in his first comments to the media after assuming office.
Reddy was inducted on Thursday into Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's cabinet, which on Tuesday cleared a proposal to introduce a bill that would end a state monopoly on broadcasting.

But the proposal, which was due to be submitted for parliamentary approval next week, was quickly opposed by the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPM), a powerful component of the 15-party United Front ruling coalition.

"The provisions in the Broadcasting BIll would lead to a situation where...the entire electronic media will be privatised with foreign media monopolies being allowed a free run," the CPM said in a statement.
"The provision for 49 percent foreign holding in media companies in India and other facilities extended to foreign satellite channels will swamp the domestic media."
The CPM is the second-largest party in the centre-left United Front alliance. It supports Gujral's government but is not represented in the cabinet.

Information and Broadcasting Ministry officials said the bill, which must be passed by parliament before it becomes law, would permit cable television stations to beam into Indian homes only if they had licences to uplink their signals from India.
It would allow foreign companies to uplink from India only in partnership with Indian firms, which would need to hold a majority of the joint venture's equity.
Satellite broadcasters, led by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp-owned Star TV, currently broadcast to India from Hong Kong and other centres.
